system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2193-03-05 22:27:00 to 2193-03-17 18:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of pancreas and kidney transplants, mechanical mitral valve replacement, and systolic heart failure was admitted for implantation of a biventricular ICD due to progressive heart failure symptoms. The procedure was performed successfully, but she developed a postoperative fever found to be due to a urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, which was treated with cefpodoxime. Her INR fluctuated during the stay, managed with heparin bridging until therapeutic on warfarin. She also experienced transient pulmonary edema, managed with diuresis. Her transplant kidney function remained stable, and she was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans in cardiology, nephrology, and primary care.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Heart valve replaced by other means

INDICATION:  ___ with end-stage renal disease, CHF, needs hemodialysis
today.  Please place right groin line catheter.  Following discussion with the
patient and referring physician, it was agreed that a tunneled right internal
jugular catheter would be appropriate.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (radiology fellow) and Dr. ___
___ (radiology attending) who was present throughout and supervised the
procedure.A member of the electrophysiology team was also present during the
case to monitor for lead displacement.

MEDICATION:  The procedure was performed under moderate conscious sedation. 
The patient received 50 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of Versed in divided doses
for a total intraservice time of 30 minutes, during which time the patient's
hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored.

RADIATION:  5 mGy, 3 minutes 35 seconds fluoroscopy time.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:

Following discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the procedure,
informed written patient consent was obtained.  The patient was brought to the
angiographic suite and placed supine on the table.  A preprocedure timeout was
performed using three patient identifiers.  The skin of the right neck and
chest was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  Approximately 4 cc
of 1% lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin and subcutaneous tissues for
local anesthesia.  Using direct ultrasound visualization, a micropuncture
needle was used to access the right internal jugular vein.  A nitinol wire
passed through the needle into the SVC.  A small skin incision was made.  The
needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.  The inner portion of the
sheath and the wire were removed and exchanged for ___ wire which passed
readily through the central veins into the right atrium and the IVC.  A
further 2 cc of 1% lidocaine was infiltrated into the skin and subcutaneous
tissues overlying the anterior chest wall medial to the pacer box.  A small
skin incision was made.  Approximately 5 cc of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine
was infiltrated along the planned tunneling route.  A 19-cm tip-to-cuff
hemodialysis catheter was selected, flushed and immersed in ortho solution. 
This was attached to a tunneling device and passed from the anterior chest
wall incision to the venotomy site.  Serial dilatation was performed over the
___ wire followed by placement of the ___ peel-away sheath.  A ___ Kumpe
catheter was passed over the wire, which was then withdrawn into the kumpe and
removed through the peel-away sheath to avoid snagging the pacer wires with
the J wire.  The catheter tubing was fed through the peel-away sheath as this
was gradually removed.  Following completion of this maneuver, the tip was in
the right atrium.  Both lumens aspirated and flushed without difficulty.  The
catheter was secured to the skin with two 0 silk sutures.  The venotomy site
was closed with subcuticular ___ Vicryl.  Steri-Strips and sterile dressings
were applied.  There were no immediate post-procedure complications.

IMPRESSION:  
Technically successful placement of a tunneled 15.5F (19cm tip to cuff) right
internal jugular hemodialysis catheter.  
The catheter is ready for use.The pacer wires were not displaced during the
case.

EXAM:  Right lower extremity Doppler ultrasound.

CLINICAL INFORMATION:  Coronary artery disease status post CABG, mechanical
valve replacement and admitted with increasing dyspnea and leg swelling.

___.

FINDINGS:  Real-time grayscale, color, and spectral Doppler sonographic
evaluation of the right common femoral, superficial femoral, popliteal veins
were performed.  There is normal compressibility, wall-to-wall color flow, and
augmentation throughout.  Color flow was seen in the posterior tibial and
peroneal veins in the right calf.  Subcutaneous edema is seen along the right
lower extremity, particularly in the popliteal region.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of deep venous thrombosis in the right lower
extremity.  Subcutaneous edema.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I know you’ve been having a hard time breathing lately. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. For the past three days, I’ve been getting short of breath just walking to the bathroom. I’ve also gained weight—up to 119 pounds from my dry weight of 112.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your legs—are they more swollen than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both legs, but my right one has always been worse. It’s getting harder to move around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. Your labs show your kidney function has worsened—creatinine is 5.6, which is higher than your baseline. That’s likely contributing to the fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my kidney again? But I’ve been taking all my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have. But sometimes, even with perfect care, the transplanted kidney can struggle. We think this is chronic allograft nephropathy. We’ll need to restart dialysis to help remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Dialysis again? I was hoping to avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s not permanent—we’re placing a temporary HD line and also a PD catheter. You’ll do hemodialysis while the PD catheter heals, then transition to peritoneal dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my heart? I’ve been so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echocardiogram shows your heart function has actually improved—from 25% to 35%. That’s good news. But you still have fluid in your lungs, which is why you’re short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the dialysis will help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Removing fluid should ease your breathing. We’ll also keep an eye on your heart valve and make sure your warfarin is managed safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray shows mild interstitial edema—fluid in the lung tissue. That confirms we’re on the right track with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CT scan? I heard you ordered one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The CT showed your transplanted kidney is stable, but there’s a small cyst near your right side. We’ll need a pelvic ultrasound later to check it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It could be harmless, but we want to be sure. Your PCP will arrange the ultrasound after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my breathing—will it get better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once dialysis starts tomorrow, you should feel improvement within a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place the HD line today. It’ll go into your neck and allow us to start dialysis tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation, so you’ll be comfortable. There might be some soreness afterward, but we’ll manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The HD line was placed successfully yesterday. You’ll start hemodialysis tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready for some relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your first dialysis session. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little dizzy, but my breathing feels a bit easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That dizziness is common after fluid removal. We’ll monitor your blood pressure and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My labs—are they improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your creatinine is coming down, and your electrolytes are stabilizing. Your infection screen was negative too—no bacteria in blood or urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried after that last UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But this time, it’s not infection—it’s fluid overload from your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to place your PD catheter in two days. It’ll let you do dialysis at home later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that require surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a minor laparoscopic procedure. You’ll be asleep, and recovery is usually quick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PD catheter was placed successfully. It’ll need about two weeks to heal before use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll keep doing HD until then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we’ll teach you how to care for the PD catheter at home—flushing and dressing changes weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing continues to improve. Lungs are clearer on exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can walk to the bathroom now without stopping. That’s a big change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent progress. Your weight is down to 115—closer to your dry weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show kidney function is stabilizing. Creatinine is now 4.3, and your acid levels are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tacrolimus level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was low at first, but now it’s in range—8.3. We’ve increased your dose to 1.5 mg in the morning and 1 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to take it on time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking about discharge in a couple of days. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted it. You’ll take 2.5 mg daily. Your PCP will manage your INR checks—next one is scheduled for next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dialysis center?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start outpatient HD tomorrow at 10:15 a.m. They’ll also flush your PD catheter and change the dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg swelling is much better. The ultrasound showed no blood clots—just fluid buildup, which is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But your circulation looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Weigh yourself every morning. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds. Take your meds as prescribed, especially tacrolimus and warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pelvic ultrasound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PCP will schedule it. It’s just to check that cyst we saw on the CT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve worked hard, and it shows. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your breathing is much better, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Remember: HD tomorrow, weigh daily, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of pancreas and kidney transplants, mechanical mitral valve replacement, and systolic heart failure was admitted for worsening dyspnea and leg swelling. She had recently completed treatment for pneumonia and was found to have acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, leading to significant fluid overload. Her heart function had improved since her last admission, with ejection fraction increasing to 35%. She was managed with hemodialysis after placement of a tunneled internal jugular catheter and underwent laparoscopic placement of a peritoneal dialysis catheter for future home dialysis. Her immunosuppressant levels were optimized, and she was restarted on warfarin. She improved clinically, with resolution of pulmonary edema and stabilization of renal function, and was discharged home to continue outpatient hemodialysis while the PD catheter matured.
